listenings.text: Team, this is a short message before Thursday. You have all read the memo, so I will not repeat the numbers. I want to say one thing about how we decide. If we choose the first option, we protect the margin this year, but we lose volume in the south, and that is a real risk. If we choose the second one, we will need more people in the analytics team, and the result will not appear before the fourth quarter. Both options are defensible. What is not defensible is a decision with no argument behind it. So on Thursday, please come with a recommendation and one number that supports it. Thank you.

Good morning, and welcome to the session. Before we open the case, a word about how these discussions work here. In this room, I am not looking for the right answer. I am looking for your reasoning. So when I ask what you would do if you were the chief executive of this company, please do not tell me what the company actually did. Tell me what you would do, and tell me why. If you disagree with the person next to you, say so. The best sessions I have seen in twenty years of teaching were the ones where two people disagreed, and both of them were right about something. Let us begin.

extra_audio.text: First, the board reads the options memo. Then it compares the two scenarios in the meeting. After that, it chooses the option with the stronger argument. Next, the finance team allocates the budget for the first quarter. Finally, the company starts the turnaround in the southern region.

paras: To the board. This memo presents two options for the southern region. We do not recommend one over the other here. We present the trade-off, and the board decides on Thursday.

Option A: protect the margin. If we hold current prices, the margin stays at last year's level, and we will not need extra headcount. However, if our main competitor cuts prices again in March, we will lose volume in six of the twelve categories, and that loss would be difficult to recover.

Option B: restructure the pricing team and rebuild the model at SKU level. If the board approved this option, we would need four more analysts and nine months of work. The turnaround would not be visible before the fourth quarter. On the other hand, if the model worked as it did in the north, we would gain a scalable system, not a one-year answer.
One last point. If we had a bigger data team today, this memo would offer three options instead of two. It does not, and the board should know that.

gist.prompt: Read once for the main idea. What is this memo really doing?
choices: Telling the board which option to choose
Showing the board a trade-off and leaving the decision to them
Explaining why the southern region will close

items: Option A does not need extra headcount.
The memo says that if prices hold, no extra headcount is needed.
Option B would show results before the fourth quarter.
The memo says the turnaround would not be visible before the fourth quarter.
The memo recommends one of the two options.
It says the board decides on Thursday; the memo only presents the trade-off.
A bigger data team would have produced three options.
The last paragraph says that with a bigger data team the memo would offer three options.
